strengths: The paper provides a clear, principled analysis of the spectral evolution of diffusion sampling (Eq. 10-12, Fig. 2), showing that low-frequency image structure converges early while high-frequency content evolves throughout sampling. This gives a well-motivated basis for making positional-encoding extrapolation time-dependent, rather than an ad hoc engineering trick.

The proposed DyPE formulation is a clean, general recipe (Eq. 13) that can be plugged into multiple existing extrapolation schemes (PI, NTK-aware, YaRN), yielding Dy-PI, Dy-NTK, and Dy-YaRN, demonstrating that the idea is not tied to one particular baseline.
The method is training-free and adds no inference-time cost, which is a meaningful practical advantage over fine-tuning-based ultra-high-resolution approaches discussed in the related work.

Empirical evaluation is fairly broad: two benchmarks (DrawBench, Aesthetic-4K) at multiple resolutions/aspect ratios, a class-conditional ImageNet experiment with FiTv2 to test generality beyond FLUX/text-to-image, a human preference study, a resolution-scaling stress test, panorama generation, and an ablation over scheduler designs (Tables 5-6) and comparison against Lumina-Next's time-aware scaled RoPE and FreeScale.

The explicit distinction from Lumina-Next's time-aware RoPE (Appendix B) is a useful contribution, clarifying that DyPE moves in the opposite direction (favoring high-frequency retention over time) and empirically outperforms it (Table 4).
weaknesses: The core spectral analysis (Eq. 10-12) is derived under a highly simplified two-term mixture with power-law image spectra and white noise, and it is unclear how well this idealized, ensemble-averaged behavior (Fig. 2a, averaged over ImageNet) generalizes to the FLUX rectified-flow model, specific prompts, or non-power-law/content-dependent regions (e.g., faces, text) that are the actual focus of the qualitative results.

Reported quantitative gains over the strongest baselines (YaRN vs Dy-YaRN) are often small (e.g., Table 1: CLIP 28.43 vs 28.17 at one resolution, FID differences of a few points that fluctuate in sign across settings), and no statistical significance or variance across seeds/multiple runs is reported, making it hard to assess whether improvements are consistent rather than noise.

The human evaluation (Table 2) uses only 20 prompts with 50 raters and reports aggregate preference percentages without inter-rater agreement statistics, confidence intervals, or details on rater screening/compensation, limiting confidence in the strength of the claimed 87-90% preference rates.

Hyperparameters λs and λt (Eq. 13) appear to require per-setting tuning (different optimal configurations found in Appendix D ablations for Dy-NTK vs Dy-YaRN), yet the main text does not clearly state how these are chosen for the primary experiments or whether they were tuned on the same benchmarks used for evaluation, raising a risk of overfitting the ablation study to the test benchmarks.

The reference list contains an unresolved placeholder citation ("Placeholder YourTeam. Fit v2: Scaling diffusion transformers... arXiv:2025.xxxxx"), suggesting incomplete manuscript preparation/proofreading before submission.

FID and other automatic metrics at ultra-high resolutions are computed after downsampling (Aesthetic-4K protocol), which may not fully capture fine-detail fidelity differences that the paper's qualitative zoom-ins emphasize as a key selling point, creating a partial mismatch between the paper's central claim (superior high-frequency detail) and the primary quantitative evidence.

The method still requires manually chosen thresholds/bands (α, β in YaRN-derived variants) and a specific parametric family κ(t)=λs·t^λt whose choice is not theoretically derived from the spectral analysis but selected empirically via grid ablation, somewhat weakening the claim that the approach is a principled, first-principles solution rather than an additional layer of tunable heuristics.

strengths: The core idea—linking the diffusion process's spectral progression (low frequencies converging early, high frequencies evolving throughout) to a time-dependent scheduling of RoPE frequency scaling—is a reasonably novel and intuitive insight that is not trivially present in prior static extrapolation schemes (PI, NTK-aware, YaRN).
The method is training-free and has no additional sampling cost, which is a practical advantage over fine-tuning-based ultra-high-resolution approaches.

The paper is broad in its empirical scope: it evaluates on DrawBench and Aesthetic-4K at multiple resolutions/aspect ratios, performs a human preference study (50 raters, pairwise comparisons), conducts a resolution-scaling-limit analysis, extends to class-conditional ImageNet generation with FiTv2, tests panoramic (extreme aspect ratio) generation, and includes an ablation over scheduler parameterizations (Appendix D).

The comparisons with Lumina-Next's time-aware scaled RoPE (Appendix B) and FreeScale (Appendix E) directly address a natural prior baseline and show the proposed scheme is conceptually distinguished (DyPE shifts emphasis from low to high frequency as sampling progresses, versus Lumina-Next's reverse direction) and empirically favorable.

Qualitative figures (zoom-ins, side-by-side comparisons) are provided to substantiate claims about fine-detail preservation, and the paper is transparent about where its advantage is more or less pronounced (e.g., larger gains in landscapes than portraits).
weaknesses: The key spectral-evolution analysis underlying the method (Fig. 2, Eq. 10-12) is derived and empirically validated using a pixel-space diffusion model trained on ImageNet, yet DyPE is deployed on FLUX, a latent diffusion transformer operating in VAE latent space. The paper does not address whether the 1/f^2 power-law and the same early-convergence-of-low-frequencies behavior actually hold in the latent space where RoPE is applied, leaving a non-trivial conceptual gap between the theoretical motivation and its practical application.

The final functional form chosen for the time-dependent scaling, κ(t) = λs·t^λt (Eq. 13), is not derived from the spectral analysis itself but is a heuristic parametric family whose two hyperparameters (λs, λt) must be tuned empirically (Appendix D/Table 5-6); this undercuts the claim of a 'principled' derivation and makes the method's quality sensitive to search over an ad hoc design space, with limited analysis of sensitivity or generality across models/resolutions beyond FLUX.

Reported FID values across almost all methods and baselines are unusually high (often 140-200), which is atypical for modern text-to-image evaluation and raises questions about the evaluation protocol (e.g., downsampling of generations for comparison with reference statistics, limited Aesthetic-4K-eval sample size of 195 pairs) and whether FID is meaningfully informative in this setting; this is not discussed or justified in the paper.

Baseline comparisons are largely restricted to static RoPE-extrapolation variants (PI, NTK-aware, YaRN) retrofit onto FLUX/FiTv2, plus one comparison to Lumina-Next's time-aware scheme and one comparison to FreeScale (built on the older SDXL/U-Net backbone, acknowledged by the authors as an unequal comparison). Several other tuning-free high-resolution methods cited in Related Work (e.g., ElasticDiffusion, AccDiffusion, HiDiffusion, ScaleCrafter, DemoFusion) are not empirically compared against, even though some could in principle be adapted to DiT backbones, leaving the claimed 'state-of-the-art' status insufficiently substantiated.

Presentation/polish issues: the reference list contains an incomplete placeholder citation ('Placeholder YourTeam. Fit v2... arXiv:2025.xxxxx'), and the human evaluation section lacks inter-rater agreement statistics or details on rater recruitment/qualification, reducing confidence in the reported preference percentages.

The human study and several ablations/comparisons largely pit each DyPE variant against its own static counterpart (e.g., NTK vs Dy-NTK, YaRN vs Dy-YaRN) rather than against the best overall baseline or other methods, which could overstate the perceived improvement relative to the strongest available alternative at each resolution.

strengths: The paper provides a clear and principled motivation based on a Fourier-space analysis of the diffusion reverse process, showing that low-frequency content converges early while high-frequency content evolves throughout sampling, and derives a 'progression map' (Eq. 12, Fig. 2b) that is used to justify the core design.
DyPE is training-free and introduces no additional sampling or inference cost, which is a practically valuable property for scaling pretrained DiTs to ultra-high resolutions.

The method is presented as a unifying, principled generalization that cleanly extends three widely used extrapolation schemes (PI, NTK-aware, YaRN) into time-aware variants (Dy-PI, Dy-NTK, Dy-YaRN) via a single family of time-parameterized scaling functions (Eq. 13), which is elegant and simplifies adoption.

Experimental coverage is broad: quantitative results across multiple resolutions/aspect ratios on DrawBench and Aesthetic-4K, a human preference study, a resolution-scaling-limit analysis, transfer to class-conditional ImageNet generation with FiTv2, panoramic image generation, and explicit comparisons to a conceptually related time-aware method (Lumina-Next) and another tuning-free baseline (FreeScale).

Consistent and increasingly pronounced improvements at higher resolutions (e.g., Fig. 5, Table 1) support the central claim that spectral-progression-aware scheduling helps more as resolution grows, which is the paper's key hypothesis.

Thorough ablation studies (Appendix D) examine alternative scheduler parameterizations (multiplicative vs. exponential, which components to time-condition) and justify the final design choices with quantitative evidence.
weaknesses: The spectral justification (1/f^ω power-law decay, Fig. 2a) is derived and empirically validated in pixel space on an ImageNet-trained diffusion model, but DyPE's main results are obtained on FLUX, which operates in a VAE latent space; the paper does not verify that the same spectral progression assumption holds in latent space, leaving a gap between the theoretical motivation and the primary experimental setting.

The 'training-free, no additional cost' framing is somewhat undercut by the need to tune two extra hyperparameters (λs, λt) per method variant; the ablation in Table 5 shows non-trivial sensitivity to these choices, suggesting some hyperparameter search is still required in practice, which is not fully acknowledged as a limitation.

Benchmark scale is modest for some evaluations (e.g., Aesthetic-4K FID uses only 195 images, and the human study uses 20 prompts/50 raters), which can make FID and preference estimates comparatively noisy, and this limitation is not discussed.

Generality beyond FLUX and FiTv2 is not demonstrated; no experiments are shown on other DiT backbones (e.g., SD3-class or other RoPE-based T2I/DiT models) to establish that the gains are architecture-agnostic.

The bibliography contains an apparent placeholder reference ('Placeholder YourTeam. Fit v2...') cited in-text as 'YourTeam, 2025', indicating incomplete proofreading/citation hygiene before submission.

The paper notes a training bias where DyPE's advantage is weaker for portrait versus landscape resolutions but does not analyze or mitigate this failure mode beyond a brief mention, leaving the method's robustness across aspect ratios only partially characterized.

strengths: The paper is grounded in a clear, quantitatively supported observation: diffusion sampling exhibits a low-to-high frequency progression (via a Fourier/PSD analysis of the mixture distribution, Eqs. 10-12, Fig. 2), which motivates a principled reason for making positional-encoding extrapolation time-dependent rather than static.

The proposed DyPE is training-free and adds no inference-time overhead, and is instantiated as simple, easily pluggable modifications (Dy-PI, Dy-NTK, Dy-YaRN) on top of three widely used extrapolation schemes, making adoption straightforward.

Evaluation breadth is a major strength: experiments span multiple benchmarks (DrawBench, Aesthetic-4K, ImageNet/FiTv2), multiple resolutions (2048² up to 6144²), multiple architectures (FLUX, Qwen-Image, FiTv2, Wan2.1 video), and multiple tasks (text-to-image, class-conditional generation, video generation, image editing, panorama generation), plus a human preference study showing consistent, often large preference margins for DyPE (70.5-94.2%).

Thorough ablations (scheduler family choices for Dy-NTK-aware and Dy-YaRN, multiplicative vs exponential scaling, attention entropy analysis) give insight into why the method works and support the design choices with evidence beyond the main results.

Good positioning relative to closely related prior work (TASR/Lumina-Next), including a specific qualitative and quantitative comparison (Table 5, Fig. 7-8) clarifying the key conceptual difference (opposite frequency-allocation strategy).
weaknesses: Improvements are not fully consistent: at the most extreme resolution reported (4096² on Aesthetic-4K), DY-YaRN's FID (186.00) is worse than plain YaRN (184.16) and worse than DY-NTK (183.72), and the resolution-scaling study (Fig. 5) shows DyPE itself degrading beyond ~4096²-6144², indicating the method's benefits are resolution-dependent and can invert at the highest resolutions tested, which is not deeply analyzed.

The core scheduler family κ(t)=λ_s·t^{λ_t} is motivated only loosely by the frequency-progression analysis; the specific functional form and its two hyperparameters are chosen via empirical ablation rather than derived from the theoretical PSD model, so the connection between Sec. 3.1's analysis and the final method is more heuristic than the paper's framing suggests.

Despite being framed as training-free with no extra cost, the method still requires hyperparameter tuning (λ_s, λ_t, and for Dy-YaRN the α, β thresholds) that appears tuned per base model/task (e.g., separate configurations quoted for FLUX vs. the video/editing/panorama extensions), raising questions about how much retuning is needed for new domains and whether reported gains are robust to this choice.

No explicit runtime/latency table is provided to substantiate the "no additional inference overhead" claim quantitatively, despite this being a central selling point relative to fine-tuning/progressive-upscaling baselines.

Code is not yet released ("will be released upon acceptance"), and while implementation details are given in the appendix, full reproducibility of the many pipeline variants (Dy-PI/Dy-NTK/Dy-YaRN, per-task hyperparameters) currently relies on the paper description alone.

The theoretical PSD derivation (Eq. 11) assumes a simple power-law natural-image spectrum and independence between noise and data terms, verified only on an ImageNet-trained denoiser (Fig. 2a), yet the method is then applied to a different pretrained flow-matching model (FLUX) and other architectures without directly re-verifying the same spectral assumptions hold there, leaving a gap between the empirical justification and the models actually evaluated.

strengths: The core motivation is grounded in a concrete empirical/theoretical observation (Fig. 2): low-frequency Fourier content of the generated sample converges early in the reverse diffusion trajectory while high-frequency content evolves throughout, and this is derived analytically under a simple mixture/PSD model (Eq. 10-12).

The proposed fix (Sec 3.2) is elegant in that it unifies PI, NTK-aware and YaRN under a single time-dependent scaling family κ(t)=λs·t^λl, requiring no retraining and no extra sampling cost, and is easy to plug into any of the three existing extrapolation schemes.

The empirical scope is unusually broad for a training-free method: text-to-image (FLUX, Qwen-Image) at multiple resolutions and aspect ratios, class-conditional generation (FiTv2), video generation (Wan2.1), image editing, and panoramic generation, together with automatic metrics (CLIP, ImageReward, Aesthetic score, FID/patch-FID/IS), a human preference study, and an attention-entropy analysis that offers a mechanistic explanation for the gains.

Ablations on scheduler design (multiplicative vs. exponential κ(t), threshold vs. NTK-term application in YaRN) are provided and show the sensitivity of the method to these choices is explored rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The derivation in Sec. 3.1/3.2 that motivates the specific parametric family κ(t)=λs·t^λl is largely heuristic: the 'unifying observation' that PI/NTK/YaRN all 'shut down' at s=1 is used to justify inserting an arbitrary power-law time dependence, but no argument is given for why a power law (versus e.g. a sigmoid or learned schedule) is the correct or optimal functional form; the choice is ultimately validated only by grid-searching a handful of discrete (λs, λt) values on the same benchmarks used for evaluation (Tables 6-7), raising a risk of benchmark-specific overfitting of hyperparameters rather than a principled, transferable recipe.

Quantitative gains are inconsistent in magnitude and occasionally absent: in Table 1 several DyPE variants show only marginal or mixed improvements over their static counterparts (e.g., DrawBench CLIP/IR at 3072×2048, or Aesthetic-4K FID at 3072×2048 where Dy-YaRN's 146.84 barely beats YaRN's 147.12), and in Table 3 DY-YaRN alone is not uniformly best (DY-YaRN+HiFlow wins global FID/IS while DY-YaRN alone wins patch-FID/patch-IS), so the paper's claim of 'consistent' improvement is stronger than the tables actually support.

No variance, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing is reported anywhere (main experiments, ablations, human study, video/editing extensions), which is particularly concerning given the small evaluation sets used (200 DrawBench prompts, 195 curated Aesthetic-4K pairs, 20-50 prompts for many ablations/appendix experiments), making it hard to judge whether reported differences (e.g., FID gaps of a few points) are meaningful or noise.

The human evaluation (Table 2) only pits DyPE variants against their own static counterparts (NTK vs Dy-NTK, TASR vs Dy-NTK, YaRN vs Dy-YaRN); it does not include comparisons against the broader set of non-PE baselines (HiFlow, UltraPixel, DiffuseHigh, etc.) evaluated automatically in Table 3, and no information is given on the number/qualification of raters or inter-rater agreement, limiting the strength of the perceptual claims.

No runtime/memory overhead measurements are reported despite the central claim of 'no additional sampling cost'; this claim is architecturally plausible (only positional encodings are modified) but is never empirically substantiated with wall-clock or memory comparisons against the baselines.

Code is not released at submission ('Code will be released upon acceptance'), and hyperparameters differ across tasks/models (e.g., λs=λt=2 for the main FLUX experiments vs. different tuned values in various ablation tables), so exact reproduction of all reported numbers would require re-deriving per-setting hyperparameters from scattered appendix tables.

The paper lacks an explicit Limitations section; the Impact Statement addresses only ethical/societal considerations, not technical limitations (e.g., failure cases beyond 6144² in Fig. 5, or scenarios where the spectral-progression assumption may not hold, such as highly stochastic or texture-dominated content).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated theoretical analysis: the paper derives a spectral 'progression map' showing that low-frequency image structure converges early in the reverse diffusion process while high-frequency detail evolves throughout, and uses this to motivate a principled, time-dependent reparameterization of existing RoPE extrapolation schemes (PI, NTK-aware, YaRN).

The proposed DyPE mechanism is training-free and adds no inference-time cost, since it only modifies how positional frequencies are scheled at each existing sampling step, making it an easy, practical drop-in for already-deployed diffusion transformers.

Extensive and diverse empirical validation: results are reported on multiple benchmarks (DrawBench, Aesthetic-4K, ImageNet via FiTv2) and resolutions (2048x3072 up to 6144^2), with both automatic metrics (CLIP, ImageReward, Aesthetic-Score, FID, patch-FID, IS) and a human preference study showing consistent and often large margins (70.5%-94.2%) in favor of DyPE variants.

Strong generalization evidence beyond the primary FLUX backbone: additional experiments on Qwen-Image, Wan2.1 video generation, high-resolution image editing, and panorama generation all show DyPE improving over static YaRN, supporting the claim that the underlying spectral-progression insight is architecture- and modality-agnostic.

Thorough ablations (Appendix D) comparing scheduler designs (multiplicative vs exponential scaling, different application points within NTK-aware/YaRN formulas) that justify the specific design choices rather than presenting them as arbitrary.

Additional mechanistic analysis (attention entropy deviation, Appendix F) offers a complementary explanation for why DyPE better preserves the pretrained model's attention structure at extrapolated resolutions.
weaknesses: The derivation of the spectral progression map relies on a simplified, isotropic 1/f^2 power-law model of natural image spectra and an independence assumption between signal and noise; while empirically supported by Fig. 2a, this is an approximation whose fidelity across diverse image content and datasets is not deeply interrogated.

Improvements in FID are sometimes marginal relative to the strongest static baseline (e.g., DY-YaRN vs YaRN at some resolutions in Table 1 differ by <1 point), so the paper's claim of consistent superiority is strongest for CLIP/ImageReward/Aesthetics but less uniformly compelling for distributional fidelity (FID).

The core scheduler hyperparameters (lambda_s, lambda_t) are selected via grid-search ablation on FLUX/DrawBench; it is not fully clear how much re-tuning (if any) was required when transferring the method to Qwen-Image and Wan2.1, leaving some open questions about hyperparameter sensitivity and transferability.
No wall-clock/runtime benchmarking is reported to substantiate the 'no additional inference cost' claim quantitatively, even though the mechanism is argued to be computationally free.

Human evaluation and some qualitative comparisons focus mainly on the DY-YaRN variant; DY-NTK-aware and DY-PI receive comparatively less perceptual validation despite being introduced as full alternatives.

The paper is very dense, with a large fraction of core comparisons, derivations, and generalization results deferred to a lengthy appendix, which can make it harder for readers to assess the full evidence base from the main text alone.
